transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-05-10
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Riley Kapoor (Redwood SE), Sanjay Rao (CTO, Nova Infotech), Maya Patel (Lead ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (VP Ops)

Summary:
Quick integration discovery focusing on SDKs and LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors, gateway/proxy patterns for enterprise, rate limits/quotas, and observability hooks for model telemetry. Customer leaning Hosted first, evaluating Dedicated/Private for compliance.

Topics:
- Redwood SDKs and REST/streaming APIs
- LangChain & LlamaIndex connectors + example workflows
- Gateway/proxy for traffic control and caching
- Rate limiting, quotas, and token accounting per route
- Observability hooks: traces, per-request metadata, token-level cost breakdowns
- Pilot plan and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Avery from Redwood. With me is Riley on the SE side. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Sanjay Rao: Good, thanks. Busy week but, uh, excited to dig in.
[00:12] Riley Kapoor: Great. Quick agenda — integration options, SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex support, and infra patterns like gateway/proxy and rate limits. Then Q&A.
[00:22] Maya Patel: Perfect. For context, we run a customer support assistant and some internal summarization jobs. Mostly streaming chat with a few batch embedding jobs. We're currently prototyping with an open model on-prem but want to evaluate Redwood Hosted to move faster.
[00:34] Liam O'Connor: And ops wants to understand what controls we get — quotas, SSO, logs, etc.
[00:39] Avery Chen: Totally. Quick question on traffic profile — what qps are you seeing and token distribution?
[00:45] Maya Patel: Right now it's small, like 5 to 10 qps on peak but if the product launches we expect spikes to 200 qps. Token length varies — most chat is short, 40‑150 tokens, but we do occasional long context like 1k tokens for document summarization.
[01:05] Riley Kapoor: That's helpful. For those volumes Hosted maps well; Dedicated if you need guaranteed throughput and isolation. Private is available for stricter compliance or VPC/on‑prem needs.
[01:18] Sanjay Rao: Can you walk us through SDKs? We use Python and Node, and a lot of our folks use LangChain.
[01:24] Avery Chen: Sure — Redwood has language SDKs (Python, Node, Go) plus a REST API. We also maintain first‑class connectors for LangChain and LlamaIndex — small adapters that let you swap in our endpoint as the llm/embeddings provider.
[01:37] Riley Kapoor: I'll share a demo repo, but the core is you import the Redwood SDK client, set api_key, then you can use RedwoodLLM in LangChain or the LlamaIndex connector. There are examples for streaming with callbacks and for embeddings with batched requests.
[01:52] Maya Patel: Any gotchas with LlamaIndex? We use it heavily for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
[01:57] Riley Kapoor: Mostly around token limits and chunking — LlamaIndex handles chunking but you need to tune chunk size to match model context. Also watch out for KV cache behavior with streaming responses; we document best practices.
[02:12] Liam O'Connor: On security — how does Hosted handle customer data? We have GDPR and some EU residency needs.
[02:19] Avery Chen: Hosted supports region selection — we have EU regions. We persist minimal logs by default; you can enable or disable persistence and redact logs. For enterprise we offer Dedicated or Private with VPC peering, KMS integration for customer‑managed keys, and SOC 2/ISO artifacts.
[02:35] Sanjay Rao: For Dedicated, is it a full GPU pool we manage? How are rollouts done?
[02:40] Riley Kapoor: Dedicated is reserved capacity with your own GPU pool managed by Redwood. You get autoscaling policies, can pin model versions, and run canary rollouts or A/B. Your data stays isolated.
[02:51] Maya Patel: We plan to do a pilot first. If we start Hosted, later move to Dedicated as load grows.
[02:56] Avery Chen: That's a common path. Now gateway/proxy — do you have an API gateway today?
[03:01] Sanjay Rao: We use an internal Kong cluster in front of our services. We could add a proxy for LLM calls.
[03:06] Riley Kapoor: Many customers use a gateway pattern to centralize auth, rate limiting, and routing. You can run our SDK client directly from backend services, or route calls through a lightweight gateway that enforces per‑team quotas and adds request metadata. The gateway can also do prefix caching for repeated prompts.
[03:22] Liam O'Connor: That prefix caching — is it on our side or Redwood side?
[03:26] Riley Kapoor: Both patterns exist. You can cache on your gateway for deterministic prompts, or rely on Redwood's KV/prefix caching that reduces compute on repeated prefixes. For some customers we do a hybrid approach.
[03:36] Maya Patel: How about rate limits and quotas? We want per‑customer and per‑team limits and token accounting.
[03:42] Avery Chen: Redwood supports per‑route and per‑api key quotas. You can set soft and hard limits, and we provide token accounting in the Console so you can see per‑token cost and latency breakdowns. For Dedicated we can enforce limits at the capacity level as well.
[03:55] Sanjay Rao: Any throttling behavior? Backoff strategy?
[03:58] Riley Kapoor: We return 429 for rate limit breaches; SDKs include retry helpers and exponential backoff. For streaming requests we also provide a graceful error and partial output if connection drops.
[04:10] Maya Patel: Observability hooks — we need traces and per‑request metadata to tie cost back to product features.
[04:16] Avery Chen: Console exposes per‑route dashboards, token‑level cost, and tracing hooks. There's a lightweight request metadata header you can add (x-redwood-metadata) and it surfaces in logs and traces. We also support OTLP forwarding so you can send spans to your tracing backend.
[04:31] Liam O'Connor: Do you capture embeddings usage separately? We want to bill different teams separately.
[04:36] Riley Kapoor: Yes, embeddings are tracked separately. You can create API keys scoped to projects or teams, and billing/usage is broken down per key/route.
[04:45] Sanjay Rao: About latency — what's realistic for 200 qps and 1k token contexts?
[04:50] Riley Kapoor: Latency depends a lot on model and quantization. For larger contexts and bigger models you see higher latency. Our runtime optimizations — KV cache, batching, kernel selection — aim to keep p99 reasonable. We can run a benchmark pilot with your sample traffic to give concrete numbers.
[05:06] Maya Patel: That would be great. Also, do you support streaming chunking callbacks into LangChain?
[05:10] Riley Kapoor: Yup, streaming is supported end‑to‑end; our LangChain connector has a stream handler that maps tokens to callbacks so agents workflows work.
[05:18] Sanjay Rao: Any limitations with LlamaIndex embeddings pipeline? We sometimes preprocess with faiss.
[05:24] Riley Kapoor: Should work fine — you can get embeddings via the SDK in batched calls to optimize throughput and then persist in Faiss. We have example notebooks.
[05:33] Liam O'Connor: For compliance, we'll need SOC2 docs and pen test reports.
[05:37] Avery Chen: We'll share SOC2 Type II and encryption docs. For Dedicated/Private we additionally provide network diagrams and can coordinate a security review.
[05:45] Sanjay Rao: On costs — do you provide recommendations for quantization or smaller variants for batch jobs?
[05:50] Riley Kapoor: Yes — Redwood Optimize gives quantization and model profile suggestions based on workload. For batch embedding jobs using a smaller quantized model can save a lot. We can run an analysis as part of the pilot.
[06:02] Maya Patel: Operational question — do you enforce token usage for streaming vs non‑streaming differently?
[06:07] Riley Kapoor: Token accounting is uniform: tokens consumed are billed. For streaming we break tokens out as they're produced but total cost is the same. You can set different routes/pricing if you want to separate streaming chat vs batch embeddings.
[06:20] Avery Chen: Quick note — if you plan to route through a gateway, we can provide a sample ingress proxy config. It shows how to forward metadata, do API key rotation, and set up local caching.
[06:31] Sanjay Rao: That's helpful.
[06:33] Liam O'Connor: What about error reporting and alerting?
[06:36] Riley Kapoor: Console has per‑route error rates, trace links, and you can plug into PagerDuty for alerts. We also can stream logs to your S3 for long term retention.
[06:45] Maya Patel: For the pilot, will you help set up telemetry hooks?
[06:48] Avery Chen: Yes — part of onboarding we help instrument request metadata and set up dashboards.
[06:54] Sanjay Rao: Ok cool. One more thing — does Redwood support model pinning for reproducible outputs?
[06:59] Riley Kapoor: Absolutely. You can pin a model version and freeze rollout so your prompts hit the same binary. We also support automatic rollbacks if quality regresses.
[07:10] Maya Patel: Any examples of customers who've switched from self‑hosted to Hosted then to Dedicated?
[07:14] Avery Chen: A few — typically startups go Hosted for speed, then move to Dedicated once traffic and compliance needs increase. We can share anonymized case studies.
[07:22] Sanjay Rao: Sounds reasonable. Let's plan the pilot.
[07:25] Avery Chen: Great — next steps are in the notes. We'll send the integration guide and SOC2 docs and Riley will set up the LangChain/LlamaIndex deep‑dive.
[07:33] Liam O'Connor: Thanks both.
[07:34] Maya Patel: Thanks.
[07:35] Avery Chen: Thanks everyone, talk soon.
